title: Early-life exposure to hardship increased risk tolerance and entrepreneurship in adulthood with gender differences.
ehr_evidence: Our study used data from multiple sources. The principal sources of information are 1) the 1990 Population Census (1% sample) for the population by county and year of birth used to estimate cohort losses; 2) the 2005 Population Mini-Census (20% sample) used to measure entrepreneurship defined in two ways— narrowly as those who owned an enterprise in the private sector and broadly to also include the self-employed; 3) the 2013 nationally representative CHFS for business ownership and risk tolerance; and 4) the China Meteorological Administration for daily instrumental temperature records at 727 stations between 1951 and 1970
summary: Quasi-experimental study using Chinese census and survey data to investigate how early-life exposure to the Great Famine affects adult entrepreneurship and risk tolerance, with a focus on gender differences and conditioning versus selection mechanisms.
key_findings: In counties where the famine was one SD more severe, women and men were 17.1% and 12.7% more likely to engage in entrepreneurship, respectively (beta=0.058, SE=0.010 for women; beta=0.111, SE=0.018 for men, P<0.01).
Among male entrepreneurs, the coefficient of famine intensity on log income was 0.724 (SE=0.169, P<0.01), while for females it was positive but not statistically significant (0.423, SE=0.279).
If hardship was one SD higher, women and men were 18.4% and 13.2% more likely to be risk tolerant, respectively.
Male entrepreneurship increased with the wife’s risk tolerance (coefficient=0.081, SE=0.023, P<0.01), but not vice versa.
Among women, neither hardship nor risk tolerance significantly increased engagement in entrepreneurship.
study_design: Quasi-experimental observational study exploiting geographical variation in famine intensity due to random weather shocks
population: Adults born before 1962 in China residing in their county of hukou registration for ≥5 years
exposure_domain: Early-life hardship (Great Famine intensity proxied by weather-induced cohort loss)
limitations: Relies on correlation between risk tolerance and ambiguity aversion rather than direct ambiguity tolerance measures.
Individual-level estimates combined effects of selective mortality and operant conditioning, potentially overestimating conditioning.
CHFS only surveyed risk tolerance of one spouse, preventing joint estimation of own and spouse's risk tolerance.
Limited quantification of the exact degree to which hardship conditioned individuals to engage in entrepreneurship.
